procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dismissing a petition to set aside the election of the respondent to the Legislative Assembly, Himachal Pradesh, from the Rohru Constituency.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text does not mention any High Court proceedings. The case went directly from the Election Tribunal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court initially heard a Civil Appeal (No. 52 of 1954) against the order of the Election Tribunal. After delivering a judgment in that appeal, the petitioner filed an application for review of that judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent, by itself, contravenes section 123(8) of the election law.

facts: An election candidate (the respondent) appointed certain government servants to act as their polling agents.
The petitioner challenged this action, arguing it constituted a major corrupt practice under section 123(8) of the election law (Act No. XLIII of 1951).
law: Section 123(8) of Act No. XLIII of 1951 prohibits corrupt practices in elections.
Section 46 of the Act, which governs the appointment of polling agents, does not contain any prohibition against appointing government servants.
This is in contrast to Section 41 of the Act, which does contain prohibitions against the appointment of certain persons as election agents.
The duties of a polling agent include ensuring ballot boxes are empty and sealed, identifying voters to prevent impersonation, and sealing packages after the poll is complete.
application: The Court analyzed the specific duties of a polling agent and concluded that they do not inherently further the election prospects of a candidate. Instead, these duties (like identifying voters and ensuring proper procedure) are aimed at preventing fraud and ensuring a fair election for all.

The Court reasoned that if the legislature had intended to disqualify government servants from acting as polling agents, it would have explicitly stated so in the statute, just as it did for election agents in a different section.

To rule that government servants are automatically disqualified would be to improperly add an exception to the law that does not exist in the text ("to engraft an exception to the statute, which is not there").

The Court distinguished between the mere act of appointment and the potential for abuse. It noted that while the appointment itself is not a violation, the situation could be different if it were proven that the candidate or their agent exploited the government servant's position to gain an unfair advantage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the appointment of a government servant as a polling agent, by itself and without more, does not contravene section 123(8) of the election law. An infringement would only occur if it was proven that the candidate abused the appointment to exploit the government servant's position for furthering their election prospects.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent, by itself, contravenes section 123(8) of the election law.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (petitioner) argued that the respondent had appointed Government servants as polling agents, and this act in itself constituted a contravention of section 123(8) of Act No. XLIII of 1951.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument, but it can be inferred from the court's ruling. The respondent would have argued that the mere appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent does not, without more, contravene section 123(8).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A disqualification for election to the Parliament under Article 102 of the Constitution also serves as a disqualification for election to the Legislatures of Part C States. A contract with the Chief Commissioner of a Part C State is considered a contract with the Central Government, which operates as a disqualification for election to both Parliament and the State's Legislative Assembly. The appointment of a government servant as a polling agent does not, by itself, contravene election law, as government servants as a class are not disqualified from acting as polling agents.
obiter: If a candidate or their agent abuses the right to appoint a government servant as a polling agent by exploiting the situation to further their election prospects, the matter can be treated as an infringement of the law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court reaffirmed its view that the mere appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent, in itself and without more, does not contravene section 123(8) of the election law. The court reasoned that to hold that Government servants are, as a class, disqualified from acting as polling agents would be to improperly add an exception to the statute where one does not exist.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation: The court applied a principle of not engrafting exceptions onto a statute that are not explicitly present in its text.

Facts and Circumstances Test: The court distinguished between a per se violation and a violation based on conduct, establishing that an infringement of section 123(8) occurs only if it is proven that the candidate or his agent abused the right to appoint a Government servant by exploiting the situation to further their election prospects.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the mere appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent is a corrupt practice was rejected because it would require the court to read a blanket disqualification into the law.
The court held that to disqualify all Government servants as a class from being polling agents would be to "engraft an exception to the statute, which is not there."
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position prevailed because the court concluded that, as an abstract proposition of law, the appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent "in itself and without more" is not an infringement of section 123(8).
The court's ruling affirmed that there is no explicit statutory bar to such an appointment.
policy_considerations: The court balanced the literal interpretation of the statute with the potential for abuse by clarifying that while the appointment itself is not illegal, it can become an infringement if the candidate or their agent exploits the Government servant's position to further their election prospects.
